newsitem.title: USA: CBOT's Arbor assures members of Project A profits.
newsitem.headline: CBOT's Arbor assures members of Project A profits.

text.p: Chicago Board of Trade (CBOT) chairman Patrick Arbor has assured members that future profits from Project A and other business ventures managed by Ceres Trading Limited Partnership would be distributed to members.
"We are taking every prudent step to ensure that our members will enjoy future financial distributions from the Project A and other Ceres divisions," Arbor wrote in a letter to members.
Surging volume this year on Project A, the CBOT's electronic after-hours trading system, has for the first time produced profits for Ceres, which was formed in March 1992.

Project A trades an average 8,500 contracts each night, above its break-even point of 4,000 contracts, which raised concerns among members about when they, as limited partners in Ceres, would receive profits, several exchange sources said.

Project A set record overnight volume of 14,918 contracts on September 3. CBOT president Thomas Donovan, speaking to European journalists on Tuesday, estimated that by the end of 1997 Project A could trade up to 20,000 contracts each night.
However, the partnership agreement is set up so that the exchange, which is the general partner, must be paid back its original investment and operational costs before profits are distributed.

Under the partnership, the members or limited partners will receive 70 percent of profits. Clearing member firms and the exchange, or general partner, will receive 20 percent and 10 percent, respectively.
Since its inception in 1994, Project A costs total $5.8 million and revenues total $4.1 million, leaving $1.7 million owed to the CBOT before profits are dispersed, Arbor wrote.
Not only is the exchange still owed $1.7 million, but, Arbor wrote, enhancements to Project A would require the exchange to lend another $3.5 million to Ceres in 1997.

"We must recognize that our collective, long-term financial interests favor reinvestment in the Project A system at this critical, early stage in order to ensure enduring growth and profitability," Arbor wrote.

Concerns from members about whether they would be paid profits surfaced in July after Ceres changed the Ceres Executive Committee to an advisory committee. Jim Cashman, a member of the committee, resigned soon after.
Peter Todebush, who represents the members as chairman of the Ceres Advisory Committee, agreed with Arbor, adding that the $3.5 million loan to Project A would improve the system.
"If we do these things right, the benefits in the long term are very immense," Todebush said in an interview.
Donovan said Project A would be upgraded and designed so CBOT members could use Project A from home on their personal computers sometime next year.
He said at the seminar that the CBOT's Marketplex page on its Internet web site was also expected to produce revenue in the future.
"I can't tell you how fast that will become a revenue stream, but everyone is looking at a way to harness it," Donovan said.

Marketplex is also managed by Ceres under its Electronic Data Division, Todebush said. Ceres is also responsible for the management of the Foreign Consultancy Department and has an option to buy the Chicago Board Brokerage system.
"They are all emerging after languishing for two or three years," Todebush said. "Project A is just one of the pieces."

Project A trades futures and options on all CBOT agricultural contracts, and on futures and options on the 30-year T-bond and 10- and five-year note. It also trades the two-year note and muni bond futures. -Derivatives desk 312-408-8750; E-mail derivatives@reuters.com
